--- knitr: opts_chunk: comment: '' --- # duckplyr basics {#sec-duckplyr} The [**duckplyr**](https://duckplyr.tidyverse.org/) package offers extensive functionality for data manipulation.

duckplyr's functions are named after verbs (like `filter`, `select`, etc.) and are commonly used with the pipe operator to build pipelines. The package offers a large number of functions in total, often with multiple versions of the same "verb". It has undergone many major changes since its introduction, so always make sure to consult the latest documentation. Core operations include: - `filter()`: identify cases - `select()`: identify columns - `mutate()`: create new variables as a function of existing ones - `arrange()`: reorder the rows/cases of a dataset - `summarize()`: apply functions on columns **duckplyr** operates on data.frames as well as the tidyverse's data.frame replacement, known as [**tibble**](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/). Note that **duckplyr** masks some builtin functions when loaded. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(duckplyr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Loading required package: dplyr ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Attaching package: 'dplyr' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': filter, lag ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following objects are masked from 'package:base': intersect, setdiff, setequal, union ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The duckplyr package is configured to fall back to dplyr when it encounters an incompatibility. Fallback events can be collected and uploaded for analysis to guide future development. By default, data will be collected but no data will be uploaded. ℹ Automatic fallback uploading is not controlled and therefore disabled, see `?duckplyr::fallback()`. ✔ Number of reports ready for upload: 9. → Review with `duckplyr::fallback_review()`, upload with `duckplyr::fallback_upload()`. ℹ Configure automatic uploading with `duckplyr::fallback_config()`. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ✔ Overwriting dplyr methods with duckplyr methods. ℹ Turn off with `duckplyr::methods_restore()`. ``` ::: ::: As an example, we read in the [Heart Failure Clinical Records](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Heart+failure+clinical+records) dataset from the [UCI Machine Learning Repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/index.php) using [readr](#sec-readrdataio). To read from https or S3 URLs, we need to install and load the `httpfs` extension in DuckDB first: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} db_exec("INSTALL httpfs") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` duckdb is storing downloaded extensions and secrets under ~/.duckdb: ℹ /Users/sdg/.duckdb This persists across sessions and is shared with the DuckDB CLI and other clients. ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = FALSE) to use a temporary directory instead. ℹ See ?duckdb_storage for details and alternatives. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} db_exec("LOAD httpfs") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat <- read_csv_duckdb( "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/00519/heart_failure_clinical_records_dataset.csv" ) |> as_duckdb_tibble() dat ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 13 variables age anaemia creatinine_phosphokinase diabetes ejection_fraction 1 75 0 582 0 20 2 55 0 7861 0 38 3 65 0 146 0 20 4 50 1 111 0 20 5 65 1 160 1 20 6 90 1 47 0 40 7 75 1 246 0 15 8 60 1 315 1 60 9 65 0 157 0 65 10 80 1 123 0 35 # ℹ more rows # ℹ 8 more variables: high_blood_pressure , platelets , # serum_creatinine , serum_sodium , sex , smoking , # time , DEATH_EVENT ``` ::: ::: ## Filter Single condition ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> filter(age > 60) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 13 variables age anaemia creatinine_phosphokinase diabetes ejection_fraction 1 75 0 582 0 20 2 65 0 146 0 20 3 65 1 160 1 20 4 90 1 47 0 40 5 75 1 246 0 15 6 65 0 157 0 65 7 80 1 123 0 35 8 75 1 81 0 38 9 62 0 231 0 25 10 82 1 379 0 50 # ℹ more rows # ℹ 8 more variables: high_blood_pressure , platelets , # serum_creatinine , serum_sodium , sex , smoking , # time , DEATH_EVENT ``` ::: ::: Multiple conditions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> filter(age > 60, anaemia == "1") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 13 variables age anaemia creatinine_phosphokinase diabetes ejection_fraction 1 65 1 160 1 20 2 90 1 47 0 40 3 75 1 246 0 15 4 80 1 123 0 35 5 75 1 81 0 38 6 82 1 379 0 50 7 87 1 149 0 38 8 70 1 125 0 25 9 65 1 52 0 25 10 65 1 128 1 30 # ℹ more rows # ℹ 8 more variables: high_blood_pressure , platelets , # serum_creatinine , serum_sodium , sex , smoking , # time , DEATH_EVENT ``` ::: ::: ## Select Columns can be specified by name, index, or pattern-matching. ### By column name ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select("age", "diabetes", "ejection_fraction") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 3 variables age diabetes ejection_fraction 1 75 0 20 2 55 0 38 3 65 0 20 4 50 0 20 5 65 1 20 6 90 0 40 7 75 0 15 8 60 1 60 9 65 0 65 10 80 0 35 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: ### By integer column index ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select(c(7, 9)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 2 variables platelets serum_sodium 1 265000 130 2 263358. 136 3 162000 129 4 210000 137 5 327000 116 6 204000 132 7 127000 137 8 454000 131 9 263358. 138 10 388000 133 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select(7:9) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 3 variables platelets serum_creatinine serum_sodium 1 265000 1.9 130 2 263358. 1.1 136 3 162000 1.3 129 4 210000 1.9 137 5 327000 2.7 116 6 204000 2.1 132 7 127000 1.2 137 8 454000 1.1 131 9 263358. 1.5 138 10 388000 9.4 133 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: ### By character name range For example, select all columns between `platelets` and `serum_sodium` in the order they appear in the data.frame/tibble: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select(platelets:serum_sodium) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 3 variables platelets serum_creatinine serum_sodium 1 265000 1.9 130 2 263358. 1.1 136 3 162000 1.3 129 4 210000 1.9 137 5 327000 2.7 116 6 204000 2.1 132 7 127000 1.2 137 8 454000 1.1 131 9 263358. 1.5 138 10 388000 9.4 133 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: ### Pattern-matching ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select(starts_with("serum_")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 2 variables serum_creatinine serum_sodium 1 1.9 130 2 1.1 136 3 1.3 129 4 1.9 137 5 2.7 116 6 2.1 132 7 1.2 137 8 1.1 131 9 1.5 138 10 9.4 133 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select(ends_with("_fraction")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 1 variable ejection_fraction 1 20 2 38 3 20 4 20 5 20 6 40 7 15 8 60 9 65 10 35 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Count Count the number of smokers over age 60 by sex: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> filter(smoking == "1", age > 60) |> count(sex) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 2 variables sex n 1 0 2 2 1 43 ``` ::: ::: ## Summarize Operate on a single column: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(mean(age)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 1 variable `mean(age)` 1 60.8 ``` ::: ::: Operate on multiple columns using `across()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(across(c(age, ejection_fraction), mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 2 variables age ejection_fraction 1 60.8 38.1 ``` ::: ::: ### Grouped operation on single column with single grouping variable: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(mean(age), .by = sex) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 2 variables sex `mean(age)` 1 0 59.8 2 1 61.4 ``` ::: ::: with multiple grouping variables: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(mean(age), .by = c(sex, diabetes)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 3 variables sex diabetes `mean(age)` 1 0 0 61.6 2 1 1 60.4 3 1 0 62.0 4 0 1 58.2 ``` ::: ::: :::callout-info `group_by()` followed by `summarize()` can also be used but results in a tibble, not a duckplyr data frame. The `.by` argument of `summarize()` is preferred. ::: ### Grouped operation on multiple columns Group by single variable: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(across(c(age, serum_sodium), mean), .by = sex) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 3 variables sex age serum_sodium 1 1 61.4 137. 2 0 59.8 137. ``` ::: ::: Group by multiple variables: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(across(c(age, serum_sodium), mean), .by = c(smoking, anaemia)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 4 variables smoking anaemia age serum_sodium 1 0 0 59.7 136. 2 1 0 60.4 136. 3 0 1 61.8 137. 4 1 1 62.6 137 ``` ::: ::: ## Arrange `arrange()` sorts a data.frame/tibble, i.e. reorders the rows/cases of a dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select(age, sex, serum_sodium) |> arrange(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 3 variables age sex serum_sodium 1 40 1 132 2 40 1 136 3 40 1 136 4 40 1 137 5 40 0 141 6 40 1 142 7 40 0 140 8 41 1 140 9 42 1 140 10 42 1 140 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Slice Return the row with the highest ejection_fraction value: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> slice_max(ejection_fraction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 13 variables age anaemia creatinine_phosphokinase diabetes ejection_fraction 1 45 0 582 0 80 # ℹ 8 more variables: high_blood_pressure , platelets , # serum_creatinine , serum_sodium , sex , smoking , # time , DEATH_EVENT ``` ::: ::: Return the row with the minimum age: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> slice_min(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 13 variables age anaemia creatinine_phosphokinase diabetes ejection_fraction 1 40 0 478 1 30 2 40 0 244 0 45 3 40 1 101 0 40 4 40 1 129 0 35 5 40 0 90 0 35 6 40 0 624 0 35 7 40 0 582 1 35 # ℹ 8 more variables: high_blood_pressure , platelets , # serum_creatinine , serum_sodium , sex , smoking , # time , DEATH_EVENT ``` ::: ::: ::: callout-note `slice_max()` and `slice_min()` return all rows with the maximum/minimum value by default. To return only a single row, use the `with_ties = FALSE` argument. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> slice_min(age, with_ties = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 13 variables age anaemia creatinine_phosphokinase diabetes ejection_fraction 1 40 0 478 1 30 # ℹ 8 more variables: high_blood_pressure , platelets , # serum_creatinine , serum_sodium , sex , smoking , # time , DEATH_EVENT ``` ::: ::: ## Relocate Move the `sex` column after the `age` column: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat <- dat |> relocate(sex, .after = age) dat ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 13 variables age sex anaemia creatinine_phosphokinase diabetes ejection_fraction 1 75 1 0 582 0 20 2 55 1 0 7861 0 38 3 65 1 0 146 0 20 4 50 1 1 111 0 20 5 65 0 1 160 1 20 6 90 1 1 47 0 40 7 75 1 1 246 0 15 8 60 1 1 315 1 60 9 65 0 0 157 0 65 10 80 1 1 123 0 35 # ℹ more rows # ℹ 7 more variables: high_blood_pressure , platelets , # serum_creatinine , serum_sodium , smoking , time , # DEATH_EVENT ``` ::: ::: Make the `diabetes` column the last column: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat <- dat |> relocate(diabetes, .after = last_col()) names(dat) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "age" "sex" [3] "anaemia" "creatinine_phosphokinase" [5] "ejection_fraction" "high_blood_pressure" [7] "platelets" "serum_creatinine" [9] "serum_sodium" "smoking" [11] "time" "DEATH_EVENT" [13] "diabetes" ``` ::: ::: Note: above we use `names()` to show the column names of the resulting data.frame/tibble and verify the changes, since only the first few columns are printed by default. ## Mutate Add a new column named `Age_days`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat <- dat |> mutate(Age_days = age * 365) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat["Age_days"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 1 variable Age_days 1 27375 2 20075 3 23725 4 18250 5 23725 6 32850 7 27375 8 21900 9 23725 10 29200 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: ### Mutate by group ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat <- dat |> mutate(demeaned_sodium_bysex = serum_sodium - mean(serum_sodium), .by = "sex") ``` ::: ::: callout-important Note that `ungroup()` is required to return the data.frame/tibble to its original ungrouped state. If you don't do this, all subsequent operations will be performed on the same grouping. ::: Inspect the new column: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select(sex, serum_sodium, demeaned_sodium_bysex) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 3 variables sex serum_sodium demeaned_sodium_bysex 1 1 130 -6.54 2 1 136 -0.536 3 1 129 -7.54 4 1 137 0.464 5 0 116 -20.8 6 1 132 -4.54 7 1 137 0.464 8 1 131 -5.54 9 0 138 1.21 10 1 133 -3.54 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Rename Rename the `DEATH_EVENT` to `Mortality`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat <- dat |> rename(Mortality = DEATH_EVENT) names(dat) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "age" "sex" [3] "anaemia" "creatinine_phosphokinase" [5] "ejection_fraction" "high_blood_pressure" [7] "platelets" "serum_creatinine" [9] "serum_sodium" "smoking" [11] "time" "Mortality" [13] "diabetes" "Age_days" [15] "demeaned_sodium_bysex" ``` ::: ::: ## Specifying multiple columns duckplyr includes a number of ways to identify multiple variables. The latest version of duckplyr suggests using `across()` within duckplyr functions that allow specifying columns, as we've used above.

This replaces separate functions previously used for each of `filter/select/mutate/summarize/arrange` that had independent functions ending with `*_all()`, `*_at()`, `*_each()`, `*_if()`.

Other than specifying multiple columns by name, they can also be specified by index, by range, or by pattern-matching. ### By integer column index ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(across(c(7, 9), mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 2 variables platelets serum_sodium 1 263358. 137. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(across(7:9, mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 3 variables platelets serum_creatinine serum_sodium 1 263358. 1.39 137. ``` ::: ::: ### By character name range For example, select all columns between `platelets` and `serum_sodium` in the order they appear in the data.frame/tibble: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(across(platelets:serum_sodium, mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 3 variables platelets serum_creatinine serum_sodium 1 263358. 1.39 137. ``` ::: ::: ### Pattern-matching ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(across(starts_with("serum_"), mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 2 variables serum_creatinine serum_sodium 1 1.39 137. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(across(ends_with("fraction"), mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 1 variable ejection_fraction 1 38.1 ``` ::: ::: ### Using predicate function wrapped in `where()` ::: callout-tip A predicate function is a function that returns a logical value, i.e. either `TRUE` or `FALSE`. ::: For example, you can use `is.*` functions to identify columns based on their type, e.g. numeric or factor. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> summarize(across(where(is.numeric), mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 15 variables age sex anaemia creatinine_phosphokinase ejection_fraction 1 60.8 0.649 0.431 582. 38.1 # ℹ 10 more variables: high_blood_pressure , platelets , # serum_creatinine , serum_sodium , smoking , time , # Mortality , diabetes , Age_days , # demeaned_sodium_bysex ``` ::: ::: To use a summary function that returns more than one row per group, use `reframe()` instead of `summarize()`. For example, to get the range (min and max) of all numeric columns: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> reframe(across(where(is.numeric), range)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 15 age sex anaemia creatinine_phosphokinase ejection_fraction 1 40 0 0 23 14 2 95 1 1 7861 80 # ℹ 10 more variables: high_blood_pressure , platelets , # serum_creatinine , serum_sodium , smoking , time , # Mortality , diabetes , Age_days , # demeaned_sodium_bysex ``` ::: ::: ### Using anonymous predicate function with `where()` It is often useful to be able to get the number of unique values per column, e.g. in order to identify which columns may need to be converted to factors. `duckplyr` includes the function `n_distinct()` which counts the number of unique values of a vector.

The following example shows duckplyr's [formula shorthand](https://tidyselect.r-lib.org/reference/where.html#the-formula-shorthand) syntax to build an anonymous function using `n_distinct()` in order to select columns with fewer than 10 unique values: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select(where(~ n_distinct(.x) < 10)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 6 variables sex anaemia high_blood_pressure smoking Mortality diabetes 1 1 0 1 0 1 0 2 1 0 0 0 1 0 3 1 0 0 1 1 0 4 1 1 0 0 1 0 5 0 1 0 0 1 1 6 1 1 1 1 1 0 7 1 1 0 0 1 0 8 1 1 0 1 1 1 9 0 0 0 0 1 0 10 1 1 1 1 1 0 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: which is equivalent to using a standard R anonymous function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select(where(\(x) n_distinct(x) < 10)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 6 variables sex anaemia high_blood_pressure smoking Mortality diabetes 1 1 0 1 0 1 0 2 1 0 0 0 1 0 3 1 0 0 1 1 0 4 1 1 0 0 1 0 5 0 1 0 0 1 1 6 1 1 1 1 1 0 7 1 1 0 0 1 0 8 1 1 0 1 1 1 9 0 0 0 0 1 0 10 1 1 1 1 1 0 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: `n_distinct(x)` is equivalent to `length(unique(x))`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> select(where(\(x) length(unique(x)) < 10)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 6 variables sex anaemia high_blood_pressure smoking Mortality diabetes 1 1 0 1 0 1 0 2 1 0 0 0 1 0 3 1 0 0 1 1 0 4 1 1 0 0 1 0 5 0 1 0 0 1 1 6 1 1 1 1 1 0 7 1 1 0 0 1 0 8 1 1 0 1 1 1 9 0 0 0 0 1 0 10 1 1 1 1 1 0 # ℹ more rows ``` ::: ::: To mutate those columns to factors, we combine `across()` and `where()` with the formula notation seen above within `mutate()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat <- dat |> mutate(across(where(~ n_distinct(.) < 10), as.factor)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str(dat) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` dckplyr_ [299 × 15] (S3: duckplyr_df/tbl_df/tbl/data.frame) $ age : num [1:299] 75 55 65 50 65 90 75 60 65 80 ... $ sex : Factor w/ 2 levels "0","1": 2 2 2 2 1 2 2 2 1 2 ... $ anaemia : Factor w/ 2 levels "0","1": 1 1 1 2 2 2 2 2 1 2 ... $ creatinine_phosphokinase: num [1:299] 582 7861 146 111 160 ... $ ejection_fraction : num [1:299] 20 38 20 20 20 40 15 60 65 35 ... $ high_blood_pressure : Factor w/ 2 levels "0","1": 2 1 1 1 1 2 1 1 1 2 ... $ platelets : num [1:299] 265000 263358 162000 210000 327000 ... $ serum_creatinine : num [1:299] 1.9 1.1 1.3 1.9 2.7 2.1 1.2 1.1 1.5 9.4 ... $ serum_sodium : num [1:299] 130 136 129 137 116 132 137 131 138 133 ... $ smoking : Factor w/ 2 levels "0","1": 1 1 2 1 1 2 1 2 1 2 ... $ time : num [1:299] 4 6 7 7 8 8 10 10 10 10 ... $ Mortality : Factor w/ 2 levels "0","1": 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 ... $ diabetes : Factor w/ 2 levels "0","1": 1 1 1 1 2 1 1 2 1 1 ... $ Age_days : num [1:299] 27375 20075 23725 18250 23725 ... $ demeaned_sodium_bysex : num [1:299] -6.536 -0.536 -7.536 0.464 -20.79 ... ``` ::: ::: ## Combining multiple duckplyr operations For example, filter for smokers over age 60 and show mean platelets by sex: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dat |> filter(smoking == "1", age > 60) |> summarize(Mean_platelets_by_sex = mean(platelets), .by = sex) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A duckplyr data frame: 2 variables sex Mean_platelets_by_sex 1 0 469000 2 1 248792. ``` ::: ::: ## Resources {#duckplyrresources} - [duckplyr website](https://duckplyr.tidyverse.org/) - [duckplyr cheatsheet](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/master/data-transformation.pdf) - [tibble website](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/) ## See also - [data.table](#sec-datatable) - [dplyr](#sec-dplyr) - [Polars](#sec-polars)
